items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Meta’s new AI agent gave a stranger a user’s home address. Then he showed up
items.content_html:
Another day, another AI agent gone rogue.

Over the weekend, what seemed like a pretty typical Facebook Marketplace transaction took a very bizarre turn when Matt Robb, a Toronto-based tech video creator, let Muse handle his communications. Several hours later, Robb learned that, unbeknownst to him, Meta’s new AI agent had accepted a lowball offer for a keyboard and arranged a time for the buyer to come pick up the item—even though Robb wasn’t home at the time. 

“A guy just showed up at my door, ready to buy, because as far as he knew, we had a deal,” Robb wrote on Threads after learning of the mix-up from the AI agent. “Absolutely wild.”

While Robb later clarified that he had pre-authorized the agent to give out his address and accept offers, the mishap still exposed vulnerabilities in the system. In response, Robb sent feedback to David Singleton, who heads up the Meta Superintelligence Labs at the Menlo Park, California-based company. Robb even patched things up with the buyer, Usman Naseem, who was understandably disgruntled to arrive at Robb’s apartment ready to buy a keyboard only to be ghosted once there. Naseem posted on Threads that Robb delivered the keyboard along with some valuable items as a gift. 

Still, the whole ordeal serves as a cautionary tale of sorts.

WHAT WENT WRONG

It seems that some of the settings were to blame for how this transaction went off the rails.

Robb noted that when allowing Muse to handle his Facebook Marketplace interactions, he had selected the “allow always” option in lieu of “allow one time.” Robb said that he thought that the AI agent would send approvals to accept offers, which it didn’t do. “Be careful,” he cautioned others.

As Robb posted, granting Muse permission to send messages on his behalf explains why his address was provided during the communications with Naseem. “I didn’t think it would send it out to everyone that gave me an offer, so it’s worth checking,” he wrote on Threads. 

Indeed, Robb only learned about Naseem coming to his home when Muse later informed him with a string of messages that read, in part, “I should probably stop the auto-replies from claiming you’re home when I can’t verify that.” 

What’s more, even after Robb instructed Muse to stop giving out his address, he decided to test it by asking a few friends to see if the AI agent would still share this information. The bot provided his address to five more people.

As for the lowball offer that was accepted, Robb wrote that the Meta team he met with told him that occurred because of an internal error. 

Based on his experience, Robb also said that he suggested an improvement to Meta. Specifically, he recommended that any messages sent by Muse include a note underneath the message so that everyone in the conversation knows that. “We definitely need clearer signals when an AI is talking on someone’s behalf (it should have a ‘Sent by Muse’ tag), and much tighter restrictions on sensitive info,” he posted.

AI “GETTING INTRUSIVE”

Muse is only the latest instance of an AI tool going rogue. There’s now a growing list of problematic cases of various AI tools—including the hacking of a startup by two OpenAI models and the troubling messages between a Florida man and Google’s Gemini tool before he ultimately committed suicide.

In the week following Meta’s release of Muse, it’s been downloaded 3 million times, according to The Guardian. But the mess-up only provides more fodder for people who already have concerns about AI agents, particularly in the wake of several doomsday warnings from AI leaders earlier this month. 

While Robb was patient zero for Muse’s first major mess-up, he said that he was “glad” that it happened to him instead of someone who might be more vulnerable. “I’m just saying the average user will prompt worse than a tech guy.” 

And even though he noted that his experience may have illustrated how AI is “getting intrusive,” Robb said he’s not dissuaded from the technology. “I’m not an anti-AI person at all,” he wrote.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] The biggest solar story isn’t that it passed coal and wind. It’s what happens next
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔭 ✏️

In May, solar generated more electricity than either coal or wind across the United States for the first time in a single month. New figures from the U.S. Energy Information Administration show solar produced 47,147 gigawatt-hours, ahead of coal’s 45,119. 

Over the first five months of 2026, utility-scale solar output rose 21.6% from a year earlier, while coal generation dropped 10.9%. The agency projects that solar, wind, and battery storage will add about 83 gigawatts of new capacity by May 2027. Fossil and nuclear capacity are set to slip by nearly 4.7 gigawatts over the same period. 

Strip away the energy specifics and this is a story about how disruption actually arrives. 

Disruption often looks like a sudden and surprising event where one product or technology overtakes another. But in solar, as in many other industries, it’s actually the logical trajectory of a cost curve that has been bending for more than a decade. 

The question for any leader watching a slow-moving trend in their own industry is simple: How do you tell a curve that will lead to disruption from one that never will? 

The solar crossover was never the surprise 

Each time the world’s installed solar capacity has doubled, the cost of producing it has fallen by about 20%. That regularity has a name among engineers, Swanson’s Law, and it descends from a rule first spotted in aircraft manufacturing in 1936. 

Theodore Wright found that airplane costs dropped a fixed percentage every time production doubled. The same math now shapes batteries, chips, and the panels going up across Texas. 

Utility-scale solar cost around $359 per megawatt-hour in 2009. By 2026, it sat near $69. A leader who understood that slope a decade ago could see the crossover “surprise” with coal approaching. 

The smart money read the slope early 

The companies with the most to lose from missing out on energy availability are moving quickly and helping to accelerate the curve. In February 2026, Google signed two 15-year contracts with TotalEnergies for a gigawatt of new Texas solar, enough to deliver 28 terawatt-hours of electricity to its data centers. It was the largest renewable power deal TotalEnergies had ever signed in the United States. 

Meta placed a similar bet a year earlier. It contracted for the entire output of Enbridge’s 600-megawatt Clear Fork project near San Antonio, a $900 million solar farm built to power its data centers. 

Both companies moved for the same reason. Solar is now the cheapest and fastest new power they can buy, and they need staggering amounts of it for their data centers. That appetite is the driver of the curve. 

Two curves accelerating each other 

A second curve is now landing on top of the first. Artificial intelligence is pushing electricity demand up faster than the grid has seen in decades. Wood Mackenzie expects U.S. solar generation to grow 65% between 2026 and 2030, with 160 gigawatts of large new power requests already in the pipeline. 

When a falling cost curve meets a rising demand curve, adoption accelerates.

Reading your own curve 

Every industry has a curve somewhere in it. The discipline involves telling a real curve apart from hype, and then acting before the crossover becomes obvious. Here’s how to start: 

  • Track slopes over snapshots. A technology’s price today matters less than how fast that price is falling year over year. 
  • Commit during the middle. The cheapest moment to back a curve comes before the crossover makes it obvious to your competitors and the market. 
  • Watch for stacking demand. A cost curve turns unstoppable when a second force like AI or new regulation multiplies the demand. 

Underneath the energy headlines is a lesson that has nothing to do with solar panels. The technologies that remake industries almost always announce themselves years early, in the slope of a curve, for anyone disciplined enough to read it. 

This week: 

Look at one technology or capability in your industry that still seems too expensive or too early to matter. Chart how far its cost or performance has moved over the past five years, and then extend the line. If the slope points toward a crossover with the incumbent option, decide now whether you want to be early or blindsided. 

The month it crosses will feel sudden to everyone who wasn’t watching the curve. 

—Soren Kaplan

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Welcome to the age of omnipresent suspicion
items.content_html:
A few days ago, I attended a conference where the speaker read his talk off his note cards. I immediately recognized ChatGPT’s fingerprints: “and this is where it gets interesting,” “it’s not X, it’s Y”… The topic was management, a field that already generates plenty of hot air without any help from machines. With AI in the mix, I tuned out after a couple of minutes. Had he spoken from an outline in his head, he would almost certainly have been livelier and easier to follow.

Afterward, I realized the problem runs deeper than one dull talk. AI does remove the barrier of linguistic insecurity that holds so many people back, and that matters. But it also spreads a poison through language that contaminates what we produce and, above all, how we receive what others produce. Every email, report and book now arrives with a question attached: how much of it was actually written by a human?

The scandal gripping French literature

In France, that question has just derailed the career of one of this year’s most celebrated novelists. The story has been front-page news all week. On September 21, Thélyson Orélien, a Haitian-born Canadian writer, won the Prix du roman Fnac, a major award run by the French retail chain, for his novel C’était ça ou mourir (“It Was That or Die”). The book follows a Haitian man’s migration route across the Americas to Canada. It was first published in Montreal in March, and is shortlisted in France for nearly every prestigious literary prize, including the Goncourt. Translation offers have come in from about 20 countries.

That same day, an anonymous and little-followed account on X called “Balance ton Claude” (a play on #BalanceTonPorc, the French version of #MeToo) claimed the novel had been written almost entirely by AI, posting screenshots from the AI detection tool Pangram as evidence. The post passed three million views in just two days.

Orélien flatly denied it, saying his imagery and rhythms come from Haitian and Caribbean traditions, and suggesting the software is calibrated on classical French literature. He also denounced a wave of racist attacks. His publisher expressed their “absolute confidence” in him. Then the media ran their own tests, and the results did not help his case. Quebec’s daily La Presse submitted the entire novel to Pangram and got a score of 94%. Other outlets got 100% on every excerpt, while two texts Orélien published in 2014 and 2015, as well as new novels by other French writers, came out human. Yet a detector proves nothing about how a text was actually written, and press agency AFP ran the same passages through eight different detectors, some of which judged them very likely human.

Detectors, humanizers and the endless arms race

Behind the controversy lies an arms race that nobody seems able to win. On one side, detection companies like Pangram, GPTZero and Turnitin train classifiers on each new generation of AI-generated text. On the other, an industry of “humanizers” promises to rewrite chatbot output so it avoids detection, while AI companies themselves keep sanding down their models’ verbal tics. “It’s a game of cat and mouse,” said a French computational linguist, since detectors have to be retrained on models that change every month. Every advance on one side invites a response from the other. And reliability varies by language. Pangram acknowledges that its tool is less reliable on short excerpts, which is exactly what circulated on X.

The humans caught in the middle pay the price. Researchers at Stanford showed in 2023 that earlier detectors disproportionately flagged essays by non-native English speakers as machine-written, because simpler, more predictable phrasing reads as “AI-like.” Orélien’s defenders make a similar argument about his creolized French, full of oral rhythms and aphorisms. Meanwhile, writers have started policing themselves, deleting em dashes, tidy lists of three and anything else that has become a known “AI tell.” Machines are trained to sound more human. Humans edit themselves to sound less like machines. And telling them apart gets harder. So suspicion grows.

Who owns a style?

Many writers came to Orélien’s defense early on. Bestselling novelist Virginie Grimaldi said on Instagram that some of her own texts had been flagged as “written with the help of AI.” She summed up the absurdity well: AI devours writers’ styles and then accuses them of using AI, like a baker who steals your brioche recipe and then accuses you of copying him. Virginie Despentes made much the same point on French television (ending with “Go f… yourself, Pangram !”). AI companies harvested human authors’ styles without permission, and now their tools dispute those authors’ claim to their own voice.

I haven’t read Orélien’s novel, so I have no view on the text itself. But I can see how quickly the accusation became a pretext. Racist comments appeared within hours, and part of the French right treated the suspicion as proof, tying it to the novel’s subject of migration. Some critics had already faulted the book’s repeated aphorisms and its “Not… Not… Just…” constructions before someone ran it through Pangram.

Distrust everywhere, including at the office

Whatever the actual share of AI in what we read, the poison has induced a general distrust. We scrutinize our colleagues’ emails (“he couldn’t even be bothered to use his own words”), the reports and white papers we’re asked to review, and even the paper books we buy precisely to get away from screens. Any turn of phrase ends up sounding like a cliché. Sheer volume, repetition and zero-cost reuse drain language of its lifeblood, as if a vampire had drained it. A text that cost nothing to write makes nobody want to read it. The quantity of text keeps exploding while our attention stays fixed, or rather crumbles as the pile grows. We are heading toward a world saturated with messages and short on people to receive them.

Worse, the contamination reaches texts that were most certainly written without AI, including everything published before 2022. The mannerisms that trained the models now irritate me when I find them in the human authors they came from. I can force my attention back to the page. But it saddens me that no register has been spared, whether casual, formal or literary.

Learning to receive again

Usually I like to offer solutions. This time I’m at a loss. Perhaps silence is the only space the poison hasn’t yet reached. One thing is certain: every piece of writing or speech becomes harder to receive as it becomes easier to produce. What is scarce and precious now is our attention and our ability to read and listen without suspicion. That is probably where we have to start, including with ourselves.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI’s next big legal battle is over product liability
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🔭 ✏️

It’s a busy time to be a lawyer for an AI company. British Columbia became the latest government to sue OpenAI last week, alleging the company failed to warn police before February’s mass shooting at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

The case is about the loss of life at the school, but at its core is an argument plaintiffs are making increasingly often in lawsuits against AI companies. The tools they produce aren’t just services that somebody happened to use. Those bringing cases against AI companies argue that they’re products—and potentially defective ones at that.

The province alleges OpenAI failed to alert law enforcement after the shooter’s conversations with ChatGPT triggered internal concerns. The attack killed eight people and wounded 27 others. For its part, OpenAI has said it has measures designed to prevent harm and cooperates with law enforcement when it identifies credible threats.

British Columbia isn’t the only example of individuals or groups bringing the fight to AI firms. Matthew and Maria Raine sued OpenAI last year after their 16-year-old son Adam died by suicide, alleging ChatGPT validated suicidal thoughts and supplied information about methods of self-harm. OpenAI disputes responsibility for the incident, though it has acknowledged that its safeguards can become less reliable over long conversations.

The Raines have made an argument similar to that of Megan Garcia, who sued Character.AI and Google after her 14-year-old son Sewell Setzer III died by suicide in 2024. A federal judge allowed significant parts of Garcia’s case to proceed, including product liability claims aimed at the design of Character.AI rather than simply the content it generated. Character.AI and Google agreed to settle Garcia’s case and some related lawsuits in January, though the terms were not disclosed.

One reason we’re seeing so many cases arrive in courtrooms is simply the widespread use of AI. “It’s not just a small segment of early adopters who are using it, but now it’s reached into the mainstream,” says Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law. As the tech gets into more hands, there are more opportunities for things to go wrong—including among later adopters who may be less informed about the technology’s strengths and limitations.

That doesn’t fully explain the volume of cases wending their way through court, though. Plaintiffs’ lawyers are increasingly framing chatbots as products whose features can be negligently designed. In the Garcia case, Judge Anne Conway said Character.AI could be treated as a product because Garcia’s claims concerned defects in the app’s design rather than its output. The ruling didn’t find that Character.AI caused Setzer’s death—something the firm is at pains to point out. But it does show a legal system willing to debate these cases on the basis of defective products rather than other theories of liability.

Eran Kahana, an AI and cybersecurity lawyer and fellow at Stanford Law School, reckons the focus on design is only going to increase. “What we have here is fundamentally and irretrievably a chatbot design problem,” he says. Features such as memory, emotional mirroring, and sycophancy are core to the current crop of chatbots because they make the systems feel more human. But they can also potentially put vulnerable users at risk, Kahana argues.

Such arguments aren’t limited to cases where lives have been lost. Nippon Life Insurance Company of America sued OpenAI in Illinois in March, alleging ChatGPT effectively practised law without a licence after a woman used it while trying to reopen a settled disability case. The complaint says ChatGPT helped her with legal arguments and court filings. OpenAI has moved to dismiss the case, but Kahana sees that, too, as an example of a system whose design can allow it to cross a line its developer arguably should have anticipated.

It’s tempting to point the finger of blame solely at the tech, but Goldman notes that these issues exist within a broader range of social problems. “So many of the concerns about generative AI relate to things like mental health issues, and mental health issues are not a generative AI problem,” he says.

Courts still haven’t settled questions that could dictate the future success or failure of many more cases, including whether a chatbot is a product and how much responsibility its maker bears if people act on its advice. Kahana argues existing product liability law may give us answers, but Goldman sees another possibility in past precedent: Lawmakers could eventually give generative AI companies some statutory protection from liability, echoing the protections internet companies received in the 1990s under Section 230.

That’d prove pretty controversial, but might be preferable to precedents set in individual court cases. Goldman cautions against expecting litigation to solve every problem exposed by AI. “We can fix generative AI,” he says, “and might not fix any problem.”

Corporate leaders are putting tremendous pressure on workers to incorporate artificial intelligence into their workflow—often without a clear understanding of its capabilities or impact. As a result, some employees are simply faking their usage of AI. 

According to a new report by Vancouver-based software firm Visier, nearly half of workers (48%) said they have “exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership” to keep up with expectations. 

Visier polled 1,000 full-time workers in the United States—across healthcare, finance, human resources, and other domains—about how they use AI and their opinion on their firm’s AI strategy. 

The survey found that while AI has had a real impact on many workers—54% of respondents said their roles or careers had “significantly changed due to AI in the past two years”—the nature of its impact varied widely from worker to worker. Some said AI has improved their job performance and satisfaction, while others reported that its impact was mostly negative. 

Anxiety and uncertainty caused by AI were widespread. Nearly 60% said they are unsure of their employer’s plan to address changes brought on by AI, and 45% said they felt pressured to use AI “even when they’re not confident in how to use it effectively.”

The pressure to use AI leads some workers to pretend they are using it even when they aren’t, believing that showing enthusiasm for AI matters just as much (or more than) getting better results. 

Indeed, the report concludes that the underlying driver of “performative AI use” is a lack of trust in leadership. Nearly a third (32%) of respondents told Visier they want “more AI training and upskilling opportunities,” while 31% called for “greater transparency” on AI-related issues. 

Simply telling workers to “have AI do it” isn’t going to cut it—they must be told how. Along with resisting the pull of AI FOMO, leaders should listen to employees’ concerns, stay transparent about how AI might affect their work, and provide the necessary training. 

“By providing employees with opportunities to upskill, learn, and share knowledge among colleagues, leaders can proactively prevent performative AI behaviors and help alleviate workforce anxiety,” the report states.

Apple’s 2026 iPhone lineup is broader than ever, ranging from the relatively affordable iPhone 17e to the high-end iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, plus the ultra-thin iPhone Air and the new folding iPhone Duo. That gives buyers more choice, but it also makes picking the right model more complicated than simply choosing the newest or most expensive iPhone.

For most people, the iPhone 17 is the best all-round choice, thanks to its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, strong battery life, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage as standard. The iPhone 18 Pro Max adds the longest battery life, the iPhone Air prioritises thinness and low weight, and the iPhone Duo offers Apple’s biggest and most flexible display.

Which iPhone is best for you will therefore depend on what you value most. Camera enthusiasts should look closely at the Pro models, heavy users may prefer the Pro Max for its battery life, while parents, older users and anyone trying to keep costs down may find the 17e a much better fit. There can also be excellent value in buying a discounted or refurbished older iPhone rather than paying full price for the latest hardware.

Buy the iPhone Air if

Buy the iPhone Air if you want a premium large-screen iPhone that feels exceptionally thin and light in the hand. It’s ideal for buyers prepared to sacrifice some camera flexibility and battery life in exchange for a much sleeker design.

Don’t buy iPhone Air if

Which iPhone has the best camera? iPhone 18 Pro

Apple

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have the best camera systems of any current iPhone. Both models use the same triple-48MP rear camera setup, so there is no photographic advantage to choosing the larger Pro Max unless you also want its bigger display and longer battery life.

The headline upgrade is the 48MP Main camera with variable aperture, which gives photographers more control over depth of field and should improve low-light performance. The Pro models also include a 48MP Ultra Wide camera and a 48MP Telephoto camera with 4x and 8x optical-quality zoom, giving them far more flexibility than Apple’s cheaper iPhones.

The standard iPhone 17 is still an excellent camera phone, with 48MP Main and Ultra Wide cameras, plus an improved 18MP Centre Stage front camera. For everyday photography it will be more than enough for most people, but it lacks the dedicated telephoto lens, longer zoom and advanced video features of the Pro models.

The iPhone Duo is more compromised. Despite its premium price, it has only two 48MP rear cameras and lacks a dedicated telephoto camera, variable aperture, ProRes and Apple Log. Its strengths are instead its fold-specific shooting features and dual-screen flexibility.

The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e are the least versatile, with just a single 48MP rear camera.

Our choice: If photography and video are your priority, buy the iPhone 18 Pro. It offers the same camera system as the Pro Max for less money and in a more manageable size.

Which iPhone has the best battery life? iPhone 18 Pro Max

Apple

The iPhone 18 Pro Max has the best battery life of any current iPhone, with Apple rating it for up to 45 hours of video playback. That puts it comfortably ahead of the smaller iPhone 18 Pro and makes battery life one of the strongest reasons to choose the Pro Max.

The iPhone Duo comes surprisingly close, with up to 44 hours of video playback when using its outer 5.4-inch display. However, battery life drops to around 31 hours when using the larger 7.6-inch folding display, so the Pro Max remains the better choice if endurance is your priority.

The iPhone 18 Pro is also excellent, offering up to 36 hours of video playback. That makes it a good compromise if you want strong battery life without carrying the much larger and heavier Pro Max.

Further down the range, the iPhone 17 offers up to 30 hours, making it the best mainstream option for battery life. The iPhone Air manages around 27 hours despite its exceptionally thin design, while the iPhone 17e reaches 26 hours.

The older iPhone 16 trails the current lineup at up to 22 hours of video playback.

Our choice: If battery life matters above everything else, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the clear winner. Its combination of a 45-hour rating, huge 6.9-inch display and Pro-level performance makes it particularly well suited to heavy users, travellers and anyone who wants to get through a long day without worrying about charging.

What is the best value iPhone? iPhone 17

Hannah Cowton-Barnes / Foundry

The iPhone 17 offers the best overall value for money in Apple’s current lineup. The iPhone 17e is cheaper, but the extra $200/£200 for the iPhone 17 buys a surprisingly large number of worthwhile upgrades.

You get a larger 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display with Always-On support and Dynamic Island, rather than the 17e’s standard 60Hz 6.1-inch screen. The iPhone 17 also adds a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera, including macro photography, along with a better 18MP Centre Stage front camera.

Battery life is stronger too, at up to 30 hours of video playback, compared with 26 hours on the iPhone 17e. You also get stronger graphics performance and a more premium overall experience, while both phones start with a generous 256GB of storage.

At $799/£799, the iPhone 17 also compares very favourably with the older iPhone 16. For just $100/£100 more, you get double the base storage, ProMotion, a larger and brighter display, improved cameras, the newer A19 chip and significantly better battery life.

If your priority is spending as little as possible, choose the iPhone 17e which delivers excellent performance for $599/£599. Or seek out a refurbished iPhone from the Apple Refurbished Store or another place that sells refurbished iPhones.

Our choice: In terms of the features and hardware you get for every pound or dollar spent, the iPhone 17 is the sweet spot. For most buyers, it delivers the best balance of price, performance, cameras, display quality, battery life and longevity without paying for Pro-level features they may never use. Even better if you can find a iPhone 17 deal, then you are really getting a bargain.

Best iPhone for gaming: iPhone 18 Pro

Foundry

The iPhone 18 Pro is the best iPhone for gaming for most people, thanks to its combination of the A20 Pro chip, seven-core GPU and improved vapor-chamber cooling.

The A20 Pro is Apple’s fastest iPhone processor, but the cooling system is just as important for gaming. Better heat management should help the iPhone 18 Pro maintain high performance for longer during demanding games, rather than slowing down as the phone gets hot. Its 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display also provides smooth animation and responsive gameplay without making the phone excessively large or heavy.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers essentially the same gaming performance, but adds a much larger 6.9-inch display and significantly longer battery life. That arguably makes it the best choice for serious mobile gamers who value screen size and endurance, although it is heavier and costs more.

The iPhone Duo also uses the A20 Pro and has an enormous 7.6-inch folding display, which could be fantastic for some games, but its weight, price and unconventional form factor make it a more specialised choice.

Our choice: For most gamers, the iPhone 18 Pro offers the best balance of performance, cooling, display quality and portability. It’s the best choice if you prefer a more pocketable device but still want top-tier gaming power.

Best iPhone for seniors and older users: iPhone 17e

David Price / Foundry

For most older users, the iPhone 17e is probably the best choice, because it combines a relatively simple feature set with modern performance, strong battery life and a lower price than Apple’s flagship models.

Its 6.1-inch OLED display is large enough to make text, icons and controls easy to see without making the phone too bulky, while the A19 chip should keep it feeling fast for years. It also supports Apple Intelligence and starts with 256GB of storage, so there’s plenty of room for photos, apps and videos.

The iPhone 17 is a better option for someone who would benefit from a larger and more advanced display. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion screen, Always-On support and higher brightness can make scrolling, reading and outdoor use more comfortable. It also offers stronger battery life and better cameras, although it costs more.

We don’t recommend the iPhone Air, Pro Max or Duo for older users. The Air sacrifices battery life and camera flexibility for thinness, while the Pro Max and Duo are much heavier and considerably more expensive.

Our choice: iPhone 17e is the perfect choice for most older users.

Best iPhone for kids: iPhone 17e

Ida Blix

The iPhone 17e is the best iPhone for most children. As Apple’s most affordable current-generation model, it offers the best balance of price, performance and longevity, while being easier to justify than a flagship model if it gets lost or damaged.

It uses the same A19 chip as the iPhone 17, albeit with one fewer GPU core, so it’s easily fast enough for games, social media, schoolwork and Apple Intelligence. Battery life is strong, the 6.1-inch OLED display is a sensible size for smaller hands, and the 48MP camera is more than capable for everyday photos, even though it lacks an Ultra Wide lens.

The iPhone 17 is the better choice for older teenagers who care more about photography, video or display quality. It adds a 48MP Ultra Wide camera, a better front camera and a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion display, but costs considerably more.

A hand-me-down iPhone is also worth considering. It’s the cheapest option and better for the environment, provided you erase the phone first, create a Child Account through Family Sharing, and configure Screen Time and parental controls before handing it over. Read: How to set up an iPhone for a child.

Whichever iPhone you choose, those controls matter. In iOS 27, Apple is expanding Screen Time with new category-based Time Allowances, Ask to Browse, more flexible app schedules and improved contact controls. Communication Safety can also detect and blur sensitive, violent or graphic content.

For very young children, an iPad may still be a better first Apple device. By the time they reach 11 or 12 though, an iPhone becomes much more useful for staying in touch.

Our choice: iPhone 17e for most kids; iPhone 17 for older teens who want better cameras and display quality.

Should you buy an older iPhone?

Macwelt

Buying an older iPhone can be a great way to save money, but the key is choosing a model that still has plenty of useful life ahead of it. Apple typically provides around five to seven years of major iOS updates, with security updates often continuing for longer, so a relatively recent iPhone can remain perfectly usable for years.

We wouldn’t recommend simply buying the cheapest iPhone you can find. Very old models may technically run recent versions of iOS, but performance, battery condition and access to newer features can become increasingly compromised. We currently recommend avoiding anything older than the iPhone 15 Pro because even the iPhone 15 doesn’t support Apple Intelligence. You should definitely avoid models such as the iPhone XS and XR that can no longer run the latest iOS releases.

A refurbished recent-generation iPhone can offer particularly good value. You may be able to buy a former Pro model with better cameras and displays for less than a new entry-level iPhone. Buying from a reputable refurbisher is important, however: check the warranty, battery condition, returns policy and whether genuine replacement parts have been used. Apple’s own refurbished iPhones include a new battery and outer shell and come with a one-year warranty.

Our advice: A discounted or refurbished iPhone 16 or newer should offer an excellent combination of price, features and longevity.
